claims.text: Adding 1–3 at% tungsten to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without tungsten.
Tungsten addition will promote solid-solution strengthening.
Tungsten addition will impede dislocation motion.
Adding 1–3 at% tungsten will enhance lattice distortion.
Adding tungsten may form fine tungsten-rich regions.
Tungsten-induced lattice distortion creates a more effective barrier to dislocation movement.
Tungsten-induced lattice distortion creates a more effective barrier to grain-boundary sliding.
The proposed barriers to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding improve high-temperature yield strength.
The proposed barriers to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding improve high-temperature creep resistance.
The tungsten-modified alloy will have higher yield strength than the tungsten-free baseline at 700–900°C.
The tungsten-modified alloy will have a lower creep rate than the tungsten-free baseline at 700–900°C.
The baseline and tungsten-modified specimens will be processed under identical melting, casting, and heat-treatment conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant yield-strength improvement, exemplified as greater than 10%, would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reduce creep rate would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the intended tungsten-induced microstructural modifications would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated high-entropy criterion requires constituent elements to be present at 5–35 at%, but the intervention introduces tungsten at only 1–3 at% while claiming to maintain that criterion. This is internally inconsistent unless tungsten is explicitly treated as a minor addition outside the five or more qualifying principal elements.
